records.name: Réunion
records.current_summary:
French equality law applies in full as an overseas department: same-sex marriage reached the island with the metropolitan statute (2013), 'sexual identity' has been a prosecutable discrimination ground in the penal code since 2012, and the national amendments that produced simplified legal gender change apply here as state law. No offence attaches to being trans, and the protection framework is actionable rather than nominal.

The audited record is honest about its thinness for this island specifically: the only territory-tied adverse documentation is framework-wide — the national detention-places watchdog found serious, persistent violations against transgender prisoners, and investigative reporting details the procedural cracks trans women prisoners fall through — both applying to the island's prisons. No local violence series, enforcement pattern, or institutional hostility programme appears in the sources, and equally no documented local support infrastructure; a small, discreet community should be assumed but is not evidenced.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of France; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): in France, where prisoners are placed by the sex on their ID under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code, transgender women held in male prisons fall into a legal grey area and are 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes' — the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. French framework applying to Réunion as a department.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 of the French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities, based on referrals since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site/document inspections, with recommendations to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. National framework covering Réunion.

PinkNews (26 Aug 2012): PM Jean-Marc Ayrault announced the same-sex marriage and adoption bill would go to the National Assembly and Senate in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge; both houses had to approve, and the Catholic Bishops Conference came out against adoption. The marriage statute that subsequently applied to Réunion with the 2013 metropolitan law.

Yagg (25 Jul 2012, French): the harassment bill adopted by the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 to add 'identité sexuelle' as a discrimination ground, making transphobia prosecutable; deputies Sergio Coronado (EELV) and Elisabeth Pochon (PS) intervened in the debate. This is the discrimination-protection basis in force in Réunion.

Yagg (19 May 2016, French): the National Assembly adopted amendment 282 — tabled by about forty Socialist deputies — inserting a Civil Code section to facilitate legal gender change for trans people, though the government's three sub-amendments could limit its scope. The gender-change framework applying to Réunion as state law.

records.name: Mayotte
records.current_summary:
On paper the fullest of regional frameworks: French civil and criminal law applies — same-sex marriage (a genuine rarity in this part of the world), gender-identity anti-discrimination protection, and legal gender change by simplified procedure following the national reforms. No law criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship.

The gap between book and life is the documented story. A 2023 report on a binational couple describes a 'long and complicated' path even to marry on this predominantly Muslim island; a legal-access directory shows no openly LGBT-friendly lawyer resident in the department (metropolitan counsel take cases); and the framework's prison findings — the state detention watchdog's report of serious violations against transgender prisoners — apply to the local jails. Social environment is conservative in a way the audited sources show through practice, not statute. For visitors, legal protection exists and enforcement of rights is slow; visibility invites social pressure more than police action.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of France; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018): trans women in France are incarcerated per their identity-document gender (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code), typically in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them, placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework binds this department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL (25 May 2021): 'persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty — based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse). Extends to local jails as French establishments.

LINFO.re (French-language report): the French National Assembly voted the simplification of legal gender change (civil-status change for trans people) — French law applies to the department, bringing the simplified procedure here. Headline-verified in cache; body largely navigation content at fetch time.

Erasing 76 Crimes (23 May 2023, Moïse Manoël-Florisse): Bruno Agar, a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte, and his Malagasy partner (pseudonym Abdallah) married at Sada Town Hall after a 'long and complicated' path — showing the gap between formal French rights and lived reality on this predominantly Muslim island. Same-sex marriage is legal here — a rarity in Africa and the Islamic world — since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975.

Avocat Gay-Friendly directory (French): no LGBT-friendly lawyer is yet referenced in Mayotte — the town list (Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada and others) returns 'we do not yet have a lawyer referenced in your region' — while Paris-based Maître Isabelle Zribi (lawyer at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law) is listed as available. Evidence of thin local legal-access infrastructure for anyone needing counsel on the island.

records.name: New Caledonia
records.current_summary:
The metropolitan civil-law framework applies to this Pacific collectivity: same-sex marriage under the 2013 statute extended here, penal-code discrimination grounds covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and judicial gender-marker change under the state's reforms. Nothing criminalises trans people or same-sex relations, and the protections read as fully national in scope.

What the audited record does not contain is territory-specific evidence in either direction: no documented local enforcement pattern, violence series, support infrastructure, or institutional programme specific to trans residents or visitors — the sources are the state-wide marriage and penal-code milestones plus the framework's prison findings (the national detention watchdog's adverse report on transgender prisoners). The practical picture is therefore one of complete formal protection in a small, close-knit society where community discretion is the reasonable assumption; this record is explicitly evidence-thin rather than affirmatively warm or hostile.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of France; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018): trans women in France are incarcerated per their legal gender marker (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code), typically in all-male facilities facing detainant assault threats, placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework applies to this collectivity's establishments as French law.

Opinion of France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL (25 May 2021): 'persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty — referrals since 2010 on some forty transgender persons plus on-site inspections (Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse; eight trans women and one trans man interviewed). Extends to establishments here as French law applies.

CNN (29 May 2013): reports France's first same-sex wedding following the 2013 marriage-equality law. French marriage law applies to this collectivity — the milestone establishing marriage availability here.

PinkNews (26 August 2012, Joseph McCormick): the French government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge — the legislative path that later extended marriage equality to this collectivity as French law.

Yagg (July 2012, French): 'identité sexuelle' (sexual identity) became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code via the sexual-harassment law — enabling prosecution of discrimination and transphobia as discrimination. French law applies to the collectivity, and the same provision was updated to read 'gender identity' in 2016.

records.name: French Polynesia
records.current_summary:
French equality law applies in full — gender-identity anti-discrimination protections since 2012, hate-crime provisions since 2017, a conversion-practice ban since 2022, and legal gender recognition without medical prerequisites — and it lands on genuinely entrenched indigenous ground: the mahuu third-gender role predates colonisation, rae-rae identities are visible in daily life across the archipelago, the territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023 with government and church participation, and travel literature calls the openness cultural rather than legal.

The undertow is real but social, not statutory: the rights overview records varying stigma, employment discrimination, and episodic transphobic violence that has pushed some rae-rae into sex work, while healthcare depth thins sharply outside the main island. For a visitor the combination is among the region's strongest — law, culture, and visibility aligned — with the standard framework caveat that the state's prison-system findings apply here too, and small-island anonymity cuts both ways.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of France; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018): in France detention follows gender marked on ID (Art. D248 separate men/women establishments) so trans women with male markers are held with men - a legal grey area. French framework applicable to French Polynesia as an overseas collectivity under French law; no Polynesia-specific content in the article.

CGLPL opinion (25 May 2021) on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: since France's Law 2016-1547 civil-status gender change no longer requires medical transition/surgery, yet no norms were added on how to house detainees accordingly - serious violations persist across French detention. French-framework treatment applicable in French Polynesia's prisons.

Grokipedia trans rights in Tahiti: gender-diverse care limited by local expertise; some trans people (raerae) face family rejection and migrate to mainland France for specialised services; mahu social role - traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity where mahu embody both male and female qualities and hold cultural standing. Care access + cultural role.

OutTraveler (4 Jul 2025): 'French Polynesia doesn't need Pride flags' - openness described as ingrained in the culture; mahu and rae-rae visible in daily life across the 118 islands; first-hand account of visiting gay couple gauging safety (Googling 'is it safe' first) finding mainstream LGBTQ+ inclusivity and pride-free acceptance. Visitor-experience picture.

RNZ Pacific: French Polynesia LGBTQIA reflection - churches round table with University of French Polynesia; Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua's government tabled a social-security Bill to fully reimburse hormonal treatment (progesterone/testosterone) like mainland France, but after heated Territorial Assembly debate the Bill failed to gain sufficient support. Concrete care-access reform failed.
Out Adventures gay travel guide for French Polynesia: 'a relaxed, gay-welcoming South Pacific culture' across Tahiti and Bora Bora's 118 islands - travel-oriented assessment of the destination.

records.name: Wallis and Futuna
records.current_summary:
The French civil and criminal framework applies: gender-identity anti-discrimination protection since 2012 and judicial gender-marker change under the 2016-17 reforms without surgery or diagnosis requirements; same-sex relations are lawful; non-binary recognition does not exist. No law criminalises trans presence.

Exposure here is shaped by scale and mores rather than statutes. The rights overview describes an isolated community of roughly eleven thousand where Catholic and Polynesian social norms create practical barriers to visibility, a traditional third-gender presence (fakafafine) coexists with stigma, there are no local gender specialists — residents travel out for any care — and anonymity in village life is close to zero. No hostile state action is documented; the only state-level adverse mechanism in evidence is the framework's own prison findings (the national detention watchdog's report). Visitors should expect personal identifiability, warm discretion, and effectively absent local institutional support.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of France; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News (Jan 2018): trans women in France whose legal gender is marked male — largely those without sex-reassignment surgery — are incarcerated in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; example of a trans woman transferred to Lille's men's facility in 2014. Relevant as the French prison framework Wallis and Futuna inherits (French law applies unless locally overridden).

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French detention, based on referrals about ~40 transgender detainees since 2010 and interviews with associations/experts; extends a 30 June 2010 opinion on trans prisoners. This French detention framework applies in Wallis and Futuna as a French collectivity.

Grokipedia compilation on transgender rights in Wallis and Futuna: French civil-law gender-marker recognition available without surgery or diagnosis since the 2016-17 French reforms; gender-identity discrimination protections since 2012 (employment, housing, services); but ~11,000 population, isolation and dominant Catholic/Polynesian norms leave practical healthcare and acceptance barriers, with fakafafine-type roles coexisting alongside stigma/concealment.

records.name: Saint Barthélemy
records.current_summary:
Under the metropolitan civil law that governs this collectivity: same-sex marriage since 2013, gender-identity anti-discrimination protections, surgery-free legal gender change, gender-affirming care available for decades, and the state's 2023 conversion-practice ban — no legal restriction touches trans or same-sex visitors, and a rights-rating page scores the territory among the region's strongest frameworks with the caveat that non-binary recognition is absent and healthcare capacity is tiny.

Visitor-facing evidence is unusually direct: verified 2026 destination guides describe a discreet luxury culture — full legal protections, 'a cosmopolitan crowd that genuinely doesn't care', no organised scene but complete safety for same-sex couples — and the rights overview reports the island attracts trans residents from less accepting neighbours. A current-status review tempers that surface: local acceptance runs lower than the visitor economy implies, though no legal regression exists. The only documented adverse mechanism remains the framework-wide prison findings. Read: protected and comfortable, shallow community depth, care requires travel.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of France; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: French prison-system reporting: the controller-general of detention places finds trans detainees — overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement — suffer the most in prison; administration policy recognises only biological sex (a 2011 Nantes case placed a trans woman in a men's prison). BLM detainees fall under this French system.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 by France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL) on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: based on ~40 referrals since 2010, it finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations applicable also to intersex and non-binary persons.

Dossier on BLM trans rights: the French framework applies — legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

Travel guide: 'full equality' under French law on ~8 square miles and ~10,000 residents; luxury-yacht economy long welcoming to gay couples with zero visible scene — discretion is the norm and same-sex couples attract no attention.

Aggregate rating 7.7/10 (9 positive rights, 1 red flag): legal gender change without surgery, anti-discrimination law in place but limited healthcare access; no government LGBT+ travel advice (FCDO shows no warnings); no trans-specific visitor tips yet submitted.

Luxury-operator guide: low crime, open and accepting culture with no Pride-specific events, staff trained for diverse guests; visitors are high-end and discreet — no LGBTQ venues or scene, but no hostility noted.

freshness_all.fact: French framework applies: marriage equality, anti-discrimination law and the 2023 conversion-practice ban; local acceptance lower, no legal regression.

records.name: Aruba
records.current_summary:
An autonomous constituent country within a Western European kingdom, Aruba legislates positively rather than merely tolerating: its parliament voted 11-5 in 2016 to open registered unions carrying married-couple benefits (pension succession, emergency medical decisions) — the first island in the Caribbean to act, by its own government's account — and the official tourism authority runs a dedicated LGBT programme marketing the island as welcoming to all visitors, with nearly a hundred nationalities resident.

Travel-culture reporting through the kingdom's networks characterises Aruba, with its two sister islands, as quiet, tolerant and mostly open — a small, stable, tourism-dependent society. The parliamentary vote's own record notes religious and cultural opposition to full equal marriage, which remains unlegislated, and no local gender-recognition or specialist-care pathway is evidenced. No enforcement against trans or same-sex visitors is documented anywhere in the record: protection by registered partnership and tourism economics rather than full equality.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of Netherlands; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: Official Aruba tourism board page marketing the island as an established LGBT destination: positions feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering, and quotes a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. Self-description by the destination's own marketer, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

Aruba's own news site (Sep 9, 2016): parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5 on Sep 8, 2016, making Aruba the first island in the Caribbean; the campaign ran 2.5 years, with openly-gay MP Desiree de Sousa-Croes as sponsor and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

GlobalGayz cultural report (edited Jan 2017): Aruba described as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curacao; notes the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands, and that same-sex adoption is legal; Catholic influence noted as the main brake.

Associated Press (Sep 9, 2016): parliament voted 11-5 with four abstentions to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights; marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognized kingdom-wide, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route; religious and cultural opposition was strong, and neither Sint Maarten nor Curacao allowed unions at the time.

records.name: Curaçao
records.current_summary:
Also an autonomous constituent country of the same kingdom, the island's audited record is one of official intent colliding with friction: representatives of all kingdom governments agreed in 2015 on an equal-rights package for Caribbean-country LGBT residents — yet the same reporting documents Pride permit difficulties as recently as 2013 and organised parliamentary opposition that the island's own government publicly opposed while supporting the community.

Travel-culture surveys place the island inside the region's quiet tolerant mainstream. For a visitor the composite reads as low legal risk with thin infrastructure: no documented state hostility, an active but negotiating community in the capital, and no evidenced local gender-recognition pathway or care capacity. The record is brief; what exists shows institutions contested rather than hostile.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of Netherlands; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: GlobalGayz (updated Jan 2017): profiles the ABC islands (Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao) as 'quiet nests of gay-friendliness' inside the Kingdom of the Netherlands; Curaçao-specific findings: it opened an LGBT 'Pink House' centre in 2010, has full autonomy except defense/foreign affairs/Supreme Court alongside Aruba, and (with Sint Maarten and Aruba) acts as driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships 8 Sept 2016 — comparator context, not Curaçao law.

Caribisch Netwerk (22 Apr 2015, Dutch): representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should quickly receive equal rights; Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels (Pueblo Soberano) publicly backed 'equal rights for everyone' despite party colleague Winifred Raveneau's fierce opposition — Raveneau had forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel via a last-minute exceptionally strict permit. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites Curaçao's IGLTA award as 'most gay welcoming in the region'; a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.
